units.name: Weather and Climate
units.summary: The difference between today’s weather and a place’s climate.

topics.name: Weather and Climate
topics.summary: Why one rainy day tells you nothing about a climate.

lessons.title: Weather and Climate Are Not the Same

objectives.text: Say why one unusual day proves nothing about climate.

keyTerms.definition: What the air is doing at one place at one time.
The usual pattern of weather in a place over many years.

sections.heading: What you will learn
sections.body: These two words are often used as if they mean the same thing. They do not, and the difference is entirely about time.

sections.heading: Weather is now
sections.body:
WEATHER is what the air is doing at one place, right now or over a few days.

    "It is raining."
    "It was hot yesterday."
    "There is wind this morning."

Weather changes quickly. It can be sunny in the morning and raining by afternoon.

sections.heading: Climate is the pattern
sections.body:
CLIMATE is what the weather is USUALLY like in a place, measured over many years — normally thirty or more.

    "This region has a rainy season and a dry season."

Climate changes slowly, over decades.

A useful way to hold the difference:

    **Weather tells you what to wear today.
    Climate tells you what clothes to own.**

One day of weather is one measurement. Climate is thousands of measurements averaged together.
sections.example:
Why one cold day proves nothing.

Someone says: "It was unusually cold last week, so the climate must be getting colder."

That does not follow. One week is weather — a single measurement.

Think of a student's marks. They score 40 on one test. Is that student weak? You cannot say from one test. They might average 80 and have had a bad day.

To judge the student you need many tests. To judge climate you need many years.

The reverse is also a mistake: one very hot week does not by itself prove the climate is warming either. Single measurements never settle questions about averages.

sections.heading: Why the difference matters
sections.body:
Farmers plan around CLIMATE — which months are usually wet decides when to plant.

They react to WEATHER — today's rain decides whether to work in the field this afternoon.

Confusing the two leads to bad decisions in both directions: planting by a single warm week, or abandoning a plan because of one unusual day.

sections.heading: Try it yourself
sections.body:
Weather or climate?
1. "It will rain this afternoon."
2. "This area is usually dry between November and March."
3. "Yesterday was the hottest day this year."
4. "This region has had heavy rains most years for the last fifty."

Then: explain in your own words why one dry month does not mean a place has a dry climate.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body:
• Weather is now or a few days; climate is the pattern over many years.
• Weather changes fast; climate changes slowly.
• Weather = what to wear today. Climate = what clothes to own.
• A single unusual day or week proves nothing about climate.

questions.question: Which statement describes CLIMATE rather than weather?
options: It is raining heavily this afternoon
This region is usually dry from November to March
There is a strong wind right now
questions.explanation: Climate is the usual pattern over many years, so "usually dry from November to March" is climate. The other three describe one day or one moment, which is weather. Weather tells you what to wear today; climate tells you what clothes to own.

questions.question: Why does one unusually cold week NOT show that a place’s climate is getting colder?
options: Because cold weeks do not count
Because climate is an average over many years, and one week is a single measurement
questions.explanation: One week is weather — a single measurement. Judging a climate from it is like judging a student from one test they did badly on. You need many years of data. Note this cuts both ways: one hot week does not prove warming either.
